content.title: About
content.content: Bitter melon (Momordica charantia) is a tropical vegetable known for its distinctive bitter taste. When cooked, the bitterness mellows while the flesh remains crisp and bright green. It is commonly stir‑fried, stewed, or boiled and added to soups, curries, and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bitter melon is cultivated in Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean.
Traditional Chinese medicine uses it to help regulate blood sugar levels.
Its green color comes from carotenoids.
Raw fruit contains cucurbitacin, a toxic compound that is destroyed by heat.
In India it is called “karela” and is often served pickled or fried.

items.title: Supports blood glucose control
items.content: Bitter melon extracts may lower post‑meal glucose spikes and improve insulin sensitivity.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Contains antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phenolics and carotenoids help protect cells from free‑radical damage.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Uncooked bitter melon contains cucurbitacin, which can cause nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Always cook before eating.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may experience skin rash or swelling after exposure.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Because it can lower blood sugar, it may amplify the effect of hypoglycemic drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the melon, remove seeds, and optionally sprinkle with salt to reduce bitterness. Then stir‑fry quickly with a little oil, add to soups, curries, or stews. Cooking softens the texture while preserving nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh melons in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a perforated bag, for up to 5‑7 days. Cooked bitter melon should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge and used within 3 days.

chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-ns-as-to.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, skinless

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh without skin are cuts of poultry meat obtained after removing the outer skin. They are high in protein, low in fat, and suitable for a wide range of cooking methods such as baking, boiling, frying, and grilling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: These cuts are staples in traditional dishes across many world cuisines.
Removing the skin reduces the fat content, making them popular among calorie‑conscious eaters.
Chicken meat is a good source of vitamin B6, which plays a role in protein metabolism.
Drumsticks and thighs contain more connective tissue, keeping them juicy when cooked properly.
Skinless meat absorbs marinades more quickly, enhancing flavor.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Skinless chicken provides about 23 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Without the skin, saturated fat levels are reduced, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, which support bone health and immune function.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The tender, skinless texture is gentle on the digestive system, especially for children and older adults.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw chicken can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Sodium in processed products
items.content: Pre‑marinated cuts may contain added salt, increasing sodium intake.

items.title: Iron overload
items.content: Large portions could contribute to excess iron intake in people with hemochromatosis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless chicken is versatile: bake, grill, boil, stew, or quickly pan‑fry. Marinate in olive oil with herbs for at least 30 minutes, then cook until golden. Baking at 200 °C (400 °F) takes 25‑30 minutes depending on piece size.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. For longer keeping, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge before cooking, not at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Collards (Brassica oleracea var. acephala) are leafy vegetables from the cruciferous family, cultivated in North Carolina (NS). When cooked they retain a bright green color, tender texture and a mildly bitter flavor. They are a staple in Southern cuisine, used in soups, stews and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards belong to the same species as cabbage, broccoli and kale.
Traditionally in the Southern United States they are cooked with smoked meat or sausage.
The leaves are rich in chlorophyll, giving them a deep green hue.
In the US they are often called “Southern kale”.
Collard seeds can be sprouted, though culinary use focuses on the leaves.

items.title: High in vitamins K and C
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked collard greens provides over 800 % of the daily value for vitamin K and about 30 % of vitamin C, supporting blood clotting and immune function.

items.title: Rich source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Calcium and magnesium contribute to strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One cup of cooked collard greens contains roughly 30 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables contain goitrogens that, in very large amounts, may affect thyroid function.

items.title: Food‑drug interactions
items.content: High vitamin K intake can reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulants such as warfarin.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook collard greens by boiling or steaming for 5‑10 minutes until tender. They can be served as a side, added to soups, stews, or braised with meat. Before cooking, rinse thoroughly and remove tough stems.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh leaves keep in the refrigerator in a perforated bag for up to 5 days. Cooked greens should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: A fresh cucumber salad sliced thin and tossed with an Italian dressing made from olive oil, vinegar, garlic, oregano, and basil. The dish offers a light, crisp texture and the aromatic notes of Mediterranean cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cucumbers are over 95% water, making the salad an excellent way to stay hydrated.
Italian dressing often includes oregano, which has antioxidant properties.
The traditional Italian "Insalata di cetrioli" is served during summer when cucumbers are at peak harvest.
Cucumber salad can accompany meat dishes or be enjoyed on its own as a light meal.
In some Italian regions, a touch of honey is added to the dressing for subtle sweetness.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Low Calorie
items.content: The salad is low in calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cucumbers provide B1, B5, and B7 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Oregano and basil are rich in polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive Support
items.content: Fiber in cucumbers promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Allergy to oregano or basil
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to the herbs used in the dressing.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the dressing is salted, monitor intake, especially for those with hypertension.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Cucumbers can carry pesticide residues; wash them thoroughly before use.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled; you can add sliced radish, cherry tomatoes, or olives. It pairs well with grilled meat, fish, or as a light appetizer.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Stir before serving to evenly distribute the dressing.

content.title: About
content.content: A chocolate doughnut with chocolate icing is a soft, fried dough treat coated in a rich chocolate glaze. It combines a lightly sweet dough flavor with the deep taste of cocoa.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chocolate doughnuts are a popular bakery item served alongside coffee.
The dough is traditionally leavened with yeast, giving the doughnut a light, airy texture.
The glaze can be made from dark, milk, or white chocolate depending on preference.
In some regions the doughnut is decorated with sprinkles, nuts, or caramel.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates provide quick energy, making the doughnut a convenient snack.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Cocoa in the chocolate glaze supplies iron, which is essential for hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate contains flavonoids that may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: If the dough is fried in partially hydrogenated oils, trans fats may be present, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Gluten and dairy allergy
items.content: Doughnuts typically contain wheat flour and dairy, which can trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Doughnuts are usually served warm and can be enjoyed as a standalone dessert or with coffee, tea, or milk. The glaze is eaten as‑is, and optional toppings like sprinkles or nuts can be added.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store doughnuts in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze them and reheat in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: A ham sandwich on white bread is a classic sandwich consisting of two slices of soft white bread with sliced cooked ham between them, often complemented by mustard, mayonnaise, lettuce, and cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded ham sandwich dates back to the 19th century in the United States.
Ham used in the sandwich is typically pork, but turkey or chicken can be substituted.
White bread provides a soft texture that lets the flavor of the ham and condiments shine.
The sandwich is a staple in school cafeterias and quick‑service cafés.
In some regions it is served with pickles or sauerkraut for extra tang.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Ham supplies high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ham is rich in vitamin B12 and niacin, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The sandwich provides quick energy from the carbohydrates in the bread and fats in the sauces.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: If cheese is added, the sandwich contributes calcium beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Fiber from lettuce
items.content: Leafy lettuce adds a modest amount of dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham is often salty, so people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Nitrites and preservatives
items.content: Some hams contain nitrites, which can be harmful in large amounts.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: White bread contains gluten and is unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Mayonnaise and cheese can make the sandwich calorie‑rich; portion control is advised.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improperly stored ham can cause foodborne illness; keep it refrigerated.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The ham sandwich is usually eaten cold, cut in half. It can be dressed with mustard, mayo, lettuce, tomato, or cucumber. For a more filling version, add a slice of cheese and a few slices of avocado.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep sliced ham wrapped tightly and refrigerated at 0‑4 °C, using it within 3‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw peppers (Capsicum spp.) are the fruits of various pepper species harvested before full ripeness. They have a bright, mildly sweet flavor and a crisp texture. Peppers are eaten fresh, added to salads, marinades, and used as aromatic ingredients in cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peppers belong to the nightshade family and are relatives of tomatoes, eggplants, and potatoes.
There are over 30 sweet pepper varieties and more than 50 hot varieties, differing in color, shape, and taste.
A single medium sweet pepper provides more than 100% of the daily vitamin C requirement for an adult.
Red, yellow and orange peppers are the same varieties allowed to fully ripen, changing color as they mature.
Peppers are a natural source of antioxidants and carotenoids.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains carotenoids
items.content: Carotenoids (beta‑carotene, lutein) help protect cells from oxidative stress and support eye health.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and folate are involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium supports fluid balance and normal heart function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peppers, manifested as skin itching or swelling.

items.title: Hot varieties
items.content: Hot peppers contain capsaicin, which can irritate the stomach and intestinal lining if consumed in excess.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Raw peppers are often treated with pesticides; thorough washing or choosing organic options is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peppers can be eaten fresh in salads, sliced for snacks, added to sandwiches, smoothies, or used in marinades. They can be lightly sautéed or roasted, but consuming them raw preserves the most vitamins.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store peppers in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, placed in a perforated bag. Properly stored, they stay fresh for 1–2 weeks. Remove any bruised or spoiled peppers to prevent spoilage of the rest.

potato-scalloped-from-dry-mix-with-meat.title: Potato Scalloped from Dry Mix with Meat

content.title: About
content.content: This ready‑to‑eat dish is a potato scalloped casserole prepared from a dry mix and enriched with pieces of meat. The mix contains spices, dried cream and starch that form a creamy sauce, while the meat adds a rich flavor and protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dry‑mix version is convenient for quick meals – just add hot water and meat.
Such mixes were traditionally used in Soviet kitchens to save time and ingredients.
Dry mixes are often fortified with B‑vitamins and iron to compensate for nutrient loss during drying.
Potatoes retain most of their starch, making the dish filling and energy‑dense.
Meat variants usually contain beef or pork, but can be adapted to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Potatoes provide slow‑release energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The added meat supplies complete protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dry mix is often enriched with thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains potassium, iron and magnesium, important for heart and muscle function.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Absence of added sugars makes the casserole suitable for moderate diets.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Dry mixes frequently contain salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Allergy to additives
items.content: Dried cream powder may trigger reactions in individuals with dairy allergies.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: When using pre‑cooked meat, ensure it is fresh to avoid food‑borne illness.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Some mixes include flavor enhancers that can cause sensitivity in certain people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dissolve the dry mix in hot water, add chopped boiled or sautéed meat, stir and bake in the oven for 20‑30 minutes until a golden crust forms. Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dry mix in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. Cool any leftovers, cover tightly and refrigerate for up to 2‑3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Powerade Zero is a low‑calorie sports drink designed to replenish electrolytes and maintain hydration during intense workouts. It contains no sugar and provides only 5 kcal per 100 ml. The drink is available in several flavors such as Lemon‑Lime, Berry Mix, and Watermelon.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Powerade Zero uses artificial sweeteners like sucralose and acesulfame‑K to keep a sweet taste without added sugar.
The formula includes electrolytes – sodium, potassium and magnesium – that help maintain fluid balance.
Powerade Zero was first launched in 2015 in response to growing demand for zero‑calorie sports beverages.
The Powerade brand is owned by The Coca‑Cola Company and is positioned as a competitor to Gatorade.
Packaging typically comes in 500 ml and 1 l plastic bottles, convenient for training and competitions.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: Electrolytes help restore fluid balance more quickly after sweat loss during exercise.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Only 5 kcal per 100 ml, making it suitable for weight‑control diets.

items.title: Sugar‑free
items.content: Prevents rapid spikes in blood glucose, important for individuals prone to diabetes.

items.title: Aids post‑workout recovery
items.content: Sodium and potassium help reduce muscle cramps and fatigue.

items.title: Convenient to consume
items.content: Easy to carry to the gym, on a run, or on a hike thanks to the portable bottle.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some people may be sensitive to sucralose or acesulfame‑K, which can cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: High sodium levels may be undesirable for individuals monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Allergy to flavorings
items.content: Certain flavors may contain additives that trigger allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drink Powerade Zero before, during, or after exercise, consuming 250‑500 ml straight or diluted with 200‑300 ml water if a milder taste is preferred. The drink can be kept refrigerated but remains stable at room temperature for several days.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bottle in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Avoid storing at temperatures above 30 °C to prevent flavor changes.
